transcript: In the 1960s, the poverty of developing countries was a problem that many developed nations preferred to ignore. In many countries of Africa, Asia and South America Hunger and disease caused people to suffer But an agricultural scientist took action Norman Borlaug He led a movement called the Green Revolution and, through the improvement of wheat varieties, succeeded in dramatically increasing the world's food production. The high-yield varieties he discovered performed well in areas with limited rainfall. In India and Mexico, wheat production doubled in a few years. Hundreds of millions of lives were saved His achievement received worldwide recognition He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970 The Green Revolution looked like a miracle But there was also criticism Monoculture, agriculture is vulnerable to pests. The use of chemical fertilizers drains the soil and lowers productivity over the long term. Borlaug himself faced these criticisms sincerely. The Green Revolution is only a temporary victory, he said. As long as the population keeps growing, the food problem will not end. Today, the world population has passed 8 billion. Without the achievements of the Green Revolution, hunger would be far worse. But new challenges are piling up. Climate change, depletion of water resources, soil exhaustion, next generation technologies such as gene edited crops are being developed. But these technologies bring new ethical issues along with them. Food security is a high priority issue that every government must confront. We must pass the lessons Borlaug left us on to the next generation.
